original_question: Which broad blood disorder, characterized by a reduced ability to carry oxygen due to low level of red blood cells, is the cause for an excessive workload on the fetal heart, resulting in a condition in the fetus characterized by an accumulation of fluid in at least two fetal compartments?

final_qi.question: Which broad blood disorder, characterized by a reduced ability to carry oxygen due to low level of red blood cells, is the cause for an excessive workload on the fetal heart, resulting in a condition in the fetus characterized by an accumulation of fluid in at least two fetal compartments?
final_qi.long_answer: Anemia – a broad blood disorder defined by a decreased red-cell mass and diminished oxygen-carrying capacity – can occur in the fetus (from causes such as Rh incompatibility, α-thalassemia, parvovirus B19 infection, etc.). The resulting fetal anemia forces the fetal heart to pump markedly increased cardiac output to maintain oxygen delivery. This high-output state ultimately overwhelms cardiac function, leading to generalized edema and effusions in at least two fetal compartments, the clinical picture known as hydrops fetalis.

final_answer.long_answer: Anemia is defined by an abnormally low red-blood-cell mass and consequently reduced oxygen-carrying capacity. When anemia develops in the fetus, the heart must pump at a much higher output to deliver adequate oxygen, which can precipitate high-output cardiac failure. This cardiac strain leads to generalized edema and the accumulation of fluid in at least two fetal compartments, the clinical picture known as hydrops fetalis.
